text:
maria: Heads up — found an exploitable flow in prod's CSV import endpoint. :rotating_light:
alex: details?
maria: The CSV importer accepts a `fetch_url` column. Backend fetches that URL via internal proxy service without org-level auth checks.
sam: oh nice catch. any evidence of exfil or just the request path? :eyes:
maria: Logs show a handful of `200` responses to internal IPs from last night 02:14-02:17 UTC. Example request:```POST /api/imports/csv HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary
...
--data 'fetch_url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/'```
irene: that's classic SSRF to metadata. Were requests authenticated as the importing user or as a system service?
maria: The proxy call runs under service identity `csv-fetcher@redwood` and we don't attach the importing user's org token for internal calls. No RBAC check on the target host.
julian: So two issues: SSRF via fetch_url + missing authz check on allowed target hosts.
sec-bot: Automated alert: unusual external-to-internal fetch pattern detected for service csv-fetcher (anomaly score 0.92).
oncall: @oncall alerted. Containment plan?
alex: Immediate actions: 1) Disable CSV import feature flag for prod. 2) Block proxy from resolving 169.254.169.254 and intranet CIDRs at egress level. 3) Rotate any service tokens that could access metadata-derived creds.
maria: I've flipped the feature flag in prod (ff: csv_import_enabled -> false) and filed a rollback in deploys.
sam: Can we add a WAF rule to drop requests with `fetch_url` pointing to private IPs?
irene: Yes but treat as defense-in-depth. Also add a strict allowlist for `fetch_url` domains (only s3.amazonaws.com and redwood-owned blob store).
julian: I'll open a task to add host validation + org-id enforcement: `imports: enforce target-host-allowlist + org-binding`
sec-bot: Incident ticket created: INC-2026-341 (severity: high).
oncall: Notify CISO and legal? Impact looks internal metadata exposure risk.
alex: Notify CISO. Also prepare an incident postmortem template: what, when, scope, exposed resources, steps taken, remediations, timeline.
maria: I've pulled the raw logs to a secure S3 bucket and started an audit log entry: ```aws s3 cp /var/log/csv_fetcher/2026-03-19.log s3://sec-audit/INC-2026-341/ --server-side-encryption aws:kms```
irene: KMS note: we should rotate the KMS key used for service token encryption if we find IAM creds were exposed. Coordinate with infra-KMS.
julian: Assigned follow-ups: @maria (log analysis + notifier), @alex (rotate service tokens + update KMS owners), @sam (WAF + proxy egress block), @irene (code patch for allowlist + RBAC checks).
sam: quick mitigation PR in flight: https://github.com/redwood-inference/imports/pull/789 — adds host validation and rejects private IPs.
oncall: Keep me posted. We'll want a customer-facing comms plan if any orgs affected.
maria: Early log analysis: no evidence of successful IAM creds retrieval, but we cannot be certain. Continuing deeper scan.
julian: After containment, schedule a canary deploy of the patched importer to a staging shard behind strict egress rules.
irene: Also add audit events for every `fetch_url` request to our audit log stream (include org_id, request_id, user_id, resolved_ip).
sec-bot: Reminder: add timeline entries and evidence links to INC-2026-341 within 24h.
alex: Will coordinate with support for possible customer outreach. Legal looped in.
maria: Thanks all, I'll update thread with any new findings. :white_check_mark:
